t.1.189.1: Long ago, in the Naimiṣa forest, the gods were holding a sacrificial session. There, O king, Vaivasvata then performed the office of slaughterer of the sacrificial victims.
t.1.189.3: Then Śakra, Varuṇa, Kubera, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Vasus and the two Aśvins, and likewise the other gods, came together there to Prajāpati, the guide of the world.
t.1.189.2: Then Yama, consecrated there for the sacrifice, O king, did not kill anyone among the creatures. So those creatures became very numerous, freed from death even as their appointed times passed by.
t.1.189.4: Then, assembled together, they said to the teacher of the world: "Through the increase of humans, a fierce fear has come upon us. Trembling at that fear and longing for ease, we all go to you for refuge."
t.1.189.5: Brahmā said: "What fear have you of human beings, when all of you are immortal? Let there never be any fear for you from mortals."
t.1.189.6: For mortals have become immortal; there is no distinction whatsoever. Troubled by this lack of distinction, we have come here for the sake of a distinction.
t.1.189.7: Vaivasvata is occupied on account of the sacrifice; it is for that reason that these men do not die. When he, single-minded, has completed all his work, then indeed the time of their end will come.
t.1.189.8: The body of Vaivasvata too, made manifest, shall be set to work by your valor; it shall be their end when the time of ending comes, for that body shall become valor among men.
t.1.189.9: Then the gods, having heard the words of the first-born god, sat down where the gods were performing sacrifice, and there those mighty ones, assembled together, saw a lotus in the Bhāgīrathī.
t.1.189.10: Seeing that, they were filled with wonder, and the valiant Indra among them went there. Then he saw a woman radiant as fire, at the place where the Gaṅgā flows forth unceasingly.
t.1.189.12: Seeing that marvel, the wielder of the thunderbolt then approached that woman and asked her from close by: "Who are you, and why do you weep? For what reason? Tell me the truth here, as you wish."
t.1.189.13: You will come to know who I am here, Śakra, and why I, ill-fated one, am weeping. Come, O king, I shall go ahead of you; you will see that on account of which I weep.
t.1.189.11: There that woman, weeping and seeking water, plunged into the goddess Gaṅgā and stood in her. A teardrop fell into the water, and there it became a golden lotus.
t.1.189.14: Then he followed her as she went, and nearby he saw a handsome youth seated on a throne, with a young woman as his companion, playing at dice on the summit of the king of mountains.
t.1.189.15: The king of the gods said to him, "Know that this whole world is under my control; I am the lord." So he spoke in anger, having seen him utterly absorbed in the dice.
t.1.189.16: But the god, seeing Śakra enraged, laughed and slowly gazed upon Śakra. Then the king of the gods was paralyzed; looked upon by him, he stood fixed like a post.
t.1.189.17: But when he had had enough of his play here, he spoke to that weeping goddess: “Let this one be brought here to where I am, close by, so that pride may never again take hold of him.”
t.1.189.18: Then Śakra, merely touched by her, fell to the earth with his limbs gone slack. The blessed lord of fierce splendor said to him: “Never again act like this in any way, Śakra.”
t.1.189.19: Roll aside this king of great mountains, for your strength and valor are immeasurable; and having opened it, enter its interior, where others like you, radiant as the sun, are dwelling.
t.1.189.20: Having opened that peak of the great mountain, he saw four others of equal splendor. Gazing upon them, he grew distressed and thought, "Surely I shall not become as these are?"
t.1.189.22: Thus addressed by the mighty lord, the king of the gods trembled violently from the humiliation, his limbs gone slack, like a leaf of the aśvattha tree shaken by the wind on the summit of the king of mountains.
t.1.189.21: Then the god Giriśa, enraged, opened wide his eyes and said to Vajrapāṇi: “Enter this cave, Śatakratu, since out of childish folly you earlier treated me with contempt.”
t.1.189.23: Thus suddenly addressed, he, trembling, with joined palms and bowed face, said this to the fierce one of many forms: “O Blessed Lord, may you today be the overseer of what remains.”
t.1.189.25: All the rest, too, shall be thus for you, there is no doubt: all of you, enter a human womb. There, having performed an irresistible deed and having brought many others to their death,
t.1.189.24: Ugradhanvan laughed and said to him, "Those of such conduct obtain no escape here; these, too, will be in the same state hereafter. Therefore enter this cave and lie down."
t.1.189.26: They shall return once more to Indra's world, most precious, which they won before by their own deeds. All this that I have spoken must be done just so, and other things as well, rich in manifold purpose.
t.1.189.27: We shall go from the world of the gods to the human world, where liberation has been ordained as hard to attain; but let the gods Dharma, Vāyu, Maghavan and the two Aśvins beget us in a mother's womb.
t.1.189.28: Having heard these words, Vajrapāṇi spoke again to the best of the gods: "For the sake of the task, I would give, from my own vigor, a man born of me to be the fifth among them."
t.1.189.30: Then, together with them, that god went to the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa, and he too arranged all of it; then they were all born upon the earth.
t.1.189.29: The Blessed One of the fierce bow, out of his graciousness, willingly granted them what they desired, just as it had been spoken. And he ordained that woman, Śrī, beloved of the world, to be their wife among men.
t.1.189.32: Those who were formerly in the form of Śakra and were confined in that cave of the northern mountain, they are these very mighty Pāṇḍavas here; and the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin is a portion of Śakra himself.
t.1.189.33: Thus, O king, were these Pāṇḍavas born, they who were formerly Indras; and Lakṣmī, appointed for them long before, is this wife of theirs, Draupadī of divine form.
t.1.189.31: And Hari plucked out two hairs, one white and the other black, saying, “Let these two hairs enter two women in the family of the Yadus, Rohiṇī and Devakī.” Of those two, one became Baladeva, and the second, the black one, came into being as Keśava.
t.1.189.34: For how else could a woman rise up from the surface of the earth at the end of a sacrificial rite, if not by divine ordinance, she whose beauty shines with the radiance of the moon and the sun, and whose exquisite fragrance spreads for the distance of a krośa?
t.1.189.35: And this other boon, O lord of men, wondrous indeed, I give you out of affection: divine sight. Behold the sons of Kuntī endowed with their holy, divine former bodies.
t.1.189.36: Then Vyāsa, the pure brahmin of supremely noble deeds, through his austerity bestowed divine sight upon that king, and the king saw them all exactly as they had been, in their former bodies.
t.1.189.37: Then he beheld them as divine beings, wearing golden diadems and garlands, resembling Śakra, radiant with the hue of fire and the sun, their chaplets bound on, handsome in form, youthful, broad-chested and tall as palm trees.
t.1.189.38: Seeing thus those handsome former Indras, shining exceedingly with spotless divine garments and with excellent golden garlands, like the three-eyed ones themselves, or the Vasus, or the divine Ādityas, endowed with every virtue, King Drupada was delighted and amazed.
t.1.189.40: Having seen that great and wondrous sight, he clasped the feet of Satyavatī's son, and with a gladdened heart he said to him, "This is no marvel in you, O supreme seer."
t.1.189.39: Having obtained that divine, immeasurable māyā, the lord of kings beheld her as well, the foremost one, like Śrī herself in embodied form, a flourishing wife worthy of them in beauty, splendor and fame.
t.1.189.41: In a penance grove there once lived a certain maiden, the daughter of a great-souled seer. But that maiden, though she was beautiful, did not find a husband.
t.1.189.42: She, it is said, pleased Śaṃkara with fierce austerity. The Lord, delighted, himself said to her, "Choose a boon."
t.1.189.43: Thus addressed, the maiden said again and again to the boon-granting god, the Lord: "I desire a husband endowed with all virtues."
t.1.189.44: Then the lord of the gods, Śaṃkara, well pleased, granted her that boon, saying, "You shall have five excellent husbands."
t.1.189.45: Propitiating the god, she then spoke these words once more: "From you I deserve a single husband endowed with virtues." Then the god of gods, pleased at heart, again spoke auspicious words to her.
t.1.189.47: O Drupada, this very one was born as your daughter, divine in form, the blameless Kṛṣṇā Pārṣatī, ordained to be the wife of the five.
t.1.189.46: Five times I was told by you again and again, 'Give me a husband.' So it shall be for you, good lady; may good fortune be yours. When you have passed into another body, it will come to pass just as was spoken.
t.1.189.48: The Śrī of heaven, arisen at the great sacrifice for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, she, having practised terrible austerity here, has come to be your daughter.
t.1.189.49: This is that lovely goddess, cherished by the gods, who through her own deeds is the one wife of the five, created by the Self-Existent himself as the consort of gods. Having heard this, O King Drupada, do as you wish.
